text.p: Potentially ground-breaking drugs for leukaemia and septic shock should help Britain's Celltech Group Plc to develop from loss-making research company into a profitable pharmaceutical business, analysts said on Wednesday.

Shares in the company have been forging ahead this year on the back of a clutch of broker recommendations, including a "stock of the year" accolade from specialist New York-based brokerage Mehta and Isaly.

Shares in Celltech have jumped 31 percent since the start of the year to close at 622-1-2 pence on Wednesday, outperforming the pharmaceutical sector by nearly 29 percent. The stock is now within sight of its May 1996 peak of 680 pence.

The company has finally shaken off a troubled image garnered in the 1980s, when it was set up with government support. Driving sentiment towards the stock is the prospect of final stage data in septic shock and leukaemia drugs in which Celltech's antibody technology plays a key part.
Greig Middleton analyst John Savin said Celltech is now in a "period of transition" from being a loss-making research company to being "a profitable, research-based niche pharmaceutical company."

Celltech chief executive Peter Fellner told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday that Phase III results from a septic shock drug being developed with Bayer AG of Germany would be released "in the early weeks of the second quarter."

The two companies hope the drug will succeed where others have failed, tackling the often fatal poisoning of the blood which sets in after surgery and other traumas. Celltech said a launch in 1998 would help put it firmly in profit in 1999.
However finance director Peter Allen told Reuters the firm expected to post a pre-tax loss of around 10 million pounds in the year to September 1997.
Even greater hopes are pinned on a product developed with American Home Products Corp which could tackle leukaemia as well as or better than chemotherapy, but without the dramatic side effects.

"The company is almost at a defining moment," Fellner said, poised between emerging as a successful pharmaceutical company if the two drugs live up to expectations or slipping back to early-stage research. Fellner said that on data published so far he was confident of success, but he refused to shake off his innate caution.

"There are upsets every month in this industry. I am cautious. If we have a current image problem it is that we are viewed as a rather cautious, conservative management," Fellner said, adding: "We keep trying to make ourselves gung-ho but we make a pretty feeble job of it because it is so alien to us."

Greig Middleton's Savin said positive news on the septic shock treatment could see the shares move into the 700 to 800 pence bracket, while analysts at Lehman Brothers see them rising to 10 pounds on positive news, and slipping back to 400 pence on bad news.
But analysts say Celltech's strength is in the pipeline, with its growing financial and technical muscle enabling it to drive harder bargains in partnerships with major drug companies.

The company is already working on a follow-up drug for septic shock that also looks promising in Crohn's disease, a poorly treated illness affecting the small intestine, and rheumatoid arthritis. Spin-offs from the leukaemia drug look promising in lung and ovarian cancer.

Celltech told Reuters it hoped to move forward this year with U.S. giant Merck & Co on a new asthma product and with Zeneca Group Plc on a drug to treat osteoarthritis, a poorly treated conditon which affects 5 million people in Britain alone.
